paragraphs.heading: What happened
paragraphs.text: At 8:32 am on May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens in Skamania County, Washington, had a catastrophic explosive eruption. It rated 5 on the volcanic explosivity index. No eruption had happened in the contiguous United States since a much smaller one at Lassen Peak in California in 1915. The 1980 eruption is often regarded as the most disastrous volcanic event in American history.

paragraphs.heading: The mountain wakes
paragraphs.text: The volcano had been dormant since its last active period in the 1840s and 1850s. Several small earthquakes starting on March 15, 1980 indicated that magma might have begun moving underneath it. On March 20 a shallow earthquake of magnitude 4.2, centered under the north flank, signaled its return. On March 27 came phreatic eruptions, which are explosions of steam caused by magma suddenly heating groundwater. They dug a new crater 250 feet wide inside the old summit crater and sent a column of ash about 7,000 feet into the air.

paragraphs.heading: A growing bulge
paragraphs.text: Magma was injected at shallow depth below the volcano, and it created a large bulge and a system of fractures on the north slope. In the last week of April a United States Geological Survey team found that a section of the north face 1.5 miles across had been pushed outward by at least 270 feet. Through the rest of April and early May the bulge grew by 5 to 6 feet a day. On April 30 geologists announced that the greatest immediate danger was the bulge area sliding, and that such a landslide might spark an eruption.

paragraphs.heading: The north face gives way
paragraphs.text: On May 18 an earthquake made the whole weakened north face slide away. This collapse was the largest landslide on land in recorded history. With the face gone, partly molten rock full of high-pressure gas and steam suddenly exploded northward toward Spirit Lake. The blast was a hot mix of lava and pulverized rock, and it overtook the landslide.

paragraphs.heading: Ash and mud
paragraphs.text: A column of erupted material rose 80,000 feet into the atmosphere and dropped ash on 11 American states and on various provinces of Canada. Meanwhile the volcano's snow and ice melted, along with several entire glaciers. The meltwater formed a series of large lahars, which are volcanic mudslides. They travelled nearly 50 miles southwest, as far as the Columbia River. The thermal energy released in the eruption equalled 26 megatons of TNT.

paragraphs.heading: The toll and what came after
paragraphs.text: About 57 people were killed, and thousands of animals died. Hundreds of square miles were turned to wasteland, with damage of over $1 billion. The mountain was left with a crater on its north side. Less severe outbursts went on into the next day, and other large eruptions, not as destructive, followed later that year. The area was later preserved in the Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument.
